# Exercise 9.3 — One toolbox for explanations: DALEX {#sec-dalex}

Exercises 9.1 and 9.2 used a different package for each explanation. The
**DALEX** package collects these methods, and more, behind one interface: you
wrap the fitted model once in an **explainer**, then ask the explainer for
whatever you want to know. The same package exists in R (with **DALEXtra**
for tidymodels) and in Python (`dalex`), with the same function names.

**Theory:** the explainer object; model performance; permutation importance
with a loss function; partial dependence and individual conditional
expectation (ceteris-paribus) profiles; break-down and SHAP explanations of one
prediction.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious,
and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not
expected to write it yourself.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "DALEX", "DALEXtra", "ranger"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(DALEX)                 # explanations for any model
library(DALEXtra)              # connects DALEX to tidymodels

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

### Part 1 — The model and the explainer

The black box is the random forest of Exercises 9.1 and 9.2: the same data
([`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv)), split and five predictors. The
predictors stay in their own units. A forest splits on one variable at a time,
so it does not need them scaled, and the plots below are easier to read in
mg/dL and years than in standard deviations.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[test_rows, ]

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)
```

Evaluate it on the test set, with the predicted classes (threshold 0.5):

```{r}
test_preds <- predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test)) |>     # adds .pred_class
  bind_cols(test)

test_preds |>
  metrics(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
```

Accuracy 0.767 and Cohen's kappa 0.459 (kappa is accuracy corrected for
the agreement expected by chance). The Python forest is grown from different
random numbers and gets 0.760 and 0.451.

Now wrap the model in an explainer. `explain_tidymodels()` needs the model,
the predictors of the data to explain it on (the 150 test patients), and the
true outcome `y` **as numbers, 1 for diabetes and 0 for none**. Give the
explainer a label; it appears on every result.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = test |> select(-diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == ______),   # 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
  label = "Random forest",
  verbose = FALSE                                # no progress report
)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = test |> select(-diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"),
  label = "Random forest",
  verbose = FALSE                                # no progress report
)
```

With `verbose = FALSE` the explainer is built silently. Leave that argument
out and it prints a report of what it found: the number of rows and columns,
and the minimum, mean and maximum of the predicted values. The check that
matters, that it predicts the probability of diabetes, is the AUC in the next
cell.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`y` must be 1 for the people with diabetes. Which level of `diabetes` is that?
Note that `as.numeric(test$diabetes)` on its own would give 1 and **2** (the
positions of the levels), and the explainer would then compare probabilities
with the wrong numbers.
:::

Ask the explainer how well the model performs:

```{r}
performance <- model_performance(explainer)
performance$measures |> as.data.frame()
```

The AUC, 0.826, is the same as `roc_auc()` gives: a quick check that the
explainer is using the probability of `pos`. Recall, precision, F1 and
accuracy use a threshold of 0.5.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- An explainer wraps a fitted model with the data to explain it on and the true outcome; every explanation is then one function call.
- The outcome must be numeric, 1 for the event and 0 otherwise; check the explainer's report and the AUC before going on.
:::

### Part 2 — Global: which variables matter?

`model_parts()` computes the **permutation importance** of Exercise 9.1:
shuffle one variable, measure how much worse the model gets, repeat
(10 times by default) and average. DALEX measures "worse" with a **loss**,
which by default for a classifier is $1 - \text{AUC}$, so a larger loss is a
worse model. Two reference rows come with the result: `_full_model_`, the loss
with nothing shuffled, and `_baseline_`, the loss when *every* variable is
shuffled at once (a model that knows nothing, AUC about 0.5).

```{r}
set.seed(1)
importance_dalex <- model_parts(explainer)

importance_dalex |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(permutation == 0) |>        # permutation 0 is the average over the 10 shuffles
  select(variable, dropout_loss)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
full_loss <- importance_dalex |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(variable == "_full_model_", permutation == 0) |>
  pull(dropout_loss)

importance_dalex |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(permutation > 0, !variable %in% c("_full_model_", "_baseline_")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dropout_loss, y = reorder(variable, dropout_loss))) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "coral", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = full_loss, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "1 - AUC after shuffling the variable (dashed: no variable shuffled)",
       y = NULL, title = "Random forest: permutation importance (DALEX)")

# DALEX's own plot gives the same picture: plot(importance_dalex)
```

The full model has a loss of 0.174 (an AUC of 0.826). Shuffling glucose
raises it to 0.334; shuffling any other variable raises it by between
0.002 (pedigree) and 0.036 (BMI). This is the ranking of Exercise 9.1, Part 3, reached with
one line of code.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- `model_parts()` is permutation importance; its loss for a classifier is 1 − AUC, so higher means the model got worse.
- `_full_model_` and `_baseline_` frame the result: the loss with nothing shuffled, and with everything shuffled.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — How does the prediction change with one variable?

An importance says *how much* a variable matters, not *how*. A
**partial dependence profile** shows how: set glucose to 60 for every test
patient, keeping everything else about them as it is, and average the
predicted probabilities; then set it to 61, and so on, up to 199. The curve of
these averages is what the model predicts, on average, at each glucose level.

One patient's curve on its own (every other variable held at her values) is
an **individual conditional expectation (ICE)** or **ceteris-paribus** profile
("all else being equal"). The partial dependence profile is the average of the
150 ICE profiles.

```{r}
pdp_glucose <- model_profile(explainer, variables = "glucose", type = "partial",
                             N = NULL,                         # use all 150 patients
                             variable_splits_type = "uniform") # an evenly spaced grid

pdp_glucose$agr_profiles |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  slice(seq(1, 101, by = 20))          # every 20th of the 101 grid points
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
pdp_glucose$agr_profiles |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `_x_`, y = `_yhat_`)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Average predicted probability of diabetes",
       title = "Partial dependence profile: glucose")

# DALEX's own plot: plot(pdp_glucose)
```

Up to a glucose of about 90 the curve stays between about 0.16 and 0.21. It
then climbs, gradually up to about 140 and steeply between 140 and 160, to
about 0.6, and stays between 0.6 and 0.66 above that. A logistic regression would have drawn a smooth S; the forest draws
steps, because it is made of splits.

Now the ICE profiles behind the average. They are stored in `cp_profiles`:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
pdp_glucose$cp_profiles |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = glucose, y = `_yhat_`, group = `_ids_`)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_glucose$agr_profiles,
            aes(x = `_x_`, y = `_yhat_`, group = NULL),
            colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Predicted probability of diabetes",
       title = "ICE profiles (grey) and their average (blue)")

# DALEX's own plot: plot(pdp_glucose, geom = "profiles")
```

**Question!** Do all the grey curves have the same shape as the blue one? What
would it mean if some went up steeply and others hardly moved?

They rise in roughly the same place but by very different amounts, and they
start at different heights. Where ICE curves have different shapes, the effect
of glucose depends on the patient's other values: an **interaction**. The
average curve hides that, which is why it is worth drawing both.

**Your turn.** Draw the partial dependence profiles for the pedigree function
and for age. `model_profile()` takes several variables at once.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pdp_more <- model_profile(explainer, variables = c(______, ______), type = "partial",
                          N = NULL, variable_splits_type = "uniform")

pdp_more$agr_profiles |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `_x_`, y = `_yhat_`)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ `_vname_`, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average predicted probability of diabetes")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
pdp_more <- model_profile(explainer, variables = c("pedigree", "age"), type = "partial",
                          N = NULL, variable_splits_type = "uniform")

pdp_more$agr_profiles |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `_x_`, y = `_yhat_`)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ `_vname_`, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average predicted probability of diabetes")
```

In both languages the average prediction rises with the pedigree function,
from about 0.3 to about 0.5, most of the rise between 0.5 and 1.3. With age
it rises from about 0.25 at 21 to about 0.45 between 40 and 55, then falls
back to about 0.35. Only 6 of the 150 test patients are over 60 (and only 3
have a pedigree function above 1.2), so the right-hand ends of both curves
rest on very few people.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A partial dependence profile is the average prediction as one variable is moved through its range, everything else about each patient held fixed.
- ICE (ceteris-paribus) profiles are the individual curves behind that average; when their shapes differ, the variable interacts with others.
- A forest's profiles are step-shaped, because the forest is made of splits.
:::

### Part 4 — One patient: break-down and SHAP

`predict_parts()` explains one prediction. Take the first test patient again,
the 28-year-old with a glucose of 194 from Exercise 9.2.

```{r}
new_observation <- test |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(-diabetes)

new_observation
predict(explainer, new_observation)          # her predicted probability
```

**SHAP**, as in Exercise 9.2. DALEX estimates the Shapley values by adding the
variables in 25 random orders and averaging each variable's contribution, with
the 150 test patients as the background:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
shap_patient <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = new_observation,
                              type = "shap", B = 25)

shap_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(B == 0) |>                    # B = 0 holds the average over the 25 orders
  select(variable, contribution) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3
shap_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(B == 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = contribution, y = reorder(variable, abs(contribution)),
             fill = contribution > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick")) +
  labs(x = "SHAP contribution to the predicted probability", y = NULL,
       title = "SHAP values for the first test patient (DALEX)")

# DALEX's own plot, with boxplots over the 25 orders: plot(shap_patient)
```

Glucose contributes +0.354, much as in Exercise 9.2 (+0.308
there). The numbers are not identical: the background is the test patients
rather than 100 training rows, and 25 random orders give an estimate, not the
exact value.

**Break-down** is the simplest way to share out a prediction: start from the
average prediction (the *intercept*), add the variables **one at a time** in a
fixed order, and record how much the average prediction moves at each step.
SHAP is the average of break-downs over many orders.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
breakdown_patient <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = new_observation,
                                   type = ______)

breakdown_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(variable, contribution, cumulative)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
breakdown_patient <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = new_observation,
                                   type = "break_down")

breakdown_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(variable, contribution, cumulative)
```

R: the intercept (the mean prediction over the 150 test patients) is 0.340;
glucose adds 0.324, then pedigree −0.013, pregnancies +0.019, age +0.076 and
BMI −0.055, ending at the prediction, 0.690. Python: intercept 0.338, glucose
+0.322, age +0.098, pregnancies −0.001, BMI +0.005, pedigree −0.073, ending
at 0.688. DALEX chooses the order itself, most influential first, so glucose
comes first in both and gets about the same contribution as its SHAP value.
The two forests order the remaining variables differently, and their
contributions change with the order.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The type is written as a string, with an underscore: look at the SHAP cell
above and at `?predict_parts`.
:::

**Question!** In the break-down, which variable comes first, and why does the
order matter? Would age get the same contribution if it were added first?

The contribution of a variable depends on what is already known when it is
added: knowing that a patient is 28 means something different before and
after you know her glucose is 194. Break-down picks one order; SHAP averages
over many, which is why it is the safer summary when variables interact.

All of these explanations, and more, can be browsed together in an
interactive dashboard:

```{r}
# Optional, not run here: an interactive dashboard of everything above
# library(modelStudio)
# modelStudio(explainer)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- `predict_parts()` explains one prediction; `type = "break_down"` adds the variables in one order, `type = "shap"` averages over many orders.
- When variables interact, a break-down depends on the order; SHAP removes that dependence by averaging.
- One explainer, four questions: how good is the model, which variables matter, how does the prediction change with a variable, and why did this patient get this prediction.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn "dalex>=1.8"

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import dalex as dx             # explanations for any model

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, cohen_kappa_score
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — The model and the explainer

The black box is the random forest of Exercises 9.1 and 9.2: the same data
([`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv)), split and five predictors. The
predictors stay in their own units. A forest splits on one variable at a time,
so it does not need them scaled, and the plots below are easier to read in
mg/dL and years than in standard deviations.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

is_test = diabetes.index % 5 == 0               # every fifth person is held back
train = diabetes[~is_test]
test  = diabetes[is_test]

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])
```

Evaluate it on the test set, with the predicted classes (threshold 0.5):

```{python}
test_class = rf.predict(test[predictors])          # predicted class, threshold 0.5

print("accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
print("kappa:   ", round(cohen_kappa_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
```

Accuracy 0.760 and Cohen's kappa 0.451 (kappa is accuracy corrected for
the agreement expected by chance). The R forest is grown from different
random numbers and gets 0.767 and 0.459.

Now wrap the model in an explainer. `dx.Explainer()` needs the model, the
predictors of the data to explain it on (the 150 test patients), and the true
outcome `y` **as numbers, 1 for diabetes and 0 for none**. Give the explainer
a label; it appears on every result.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
explainer = dx.Explainer(
    rf,
    data=test[______],
    y=test["diabetes"],                           # already 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
    label="Random forest",
    verbose=False,                                # no progress report
)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
explainer = dx.Explainer(
    rf,
    data=test[predictors],
    y=test["diabetes"],
    label="Random forest",
    verbose=False,                                # no progress report
)
```

With `verbose = FALSE` the explainer is built silently. Leave that argument
out and it prints a report of what it found: the number of rows and columns,
and the minimum, mean and maximum of the predicted values. The check that
matters, that it predicts the probability of diabetes, is the AUC in the next
cell.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`data` is the table of predictors only, without the outcome column: the same
columns the forest was fitted on.
:::

Ask the explainer how well the model performs:

```{python}
performance = explainer.model_performance()
performance.result.round(3)
```

The AUC, 0.824, is the same as `roc_auc_score()` gives on these
probabilities: a quick check that the explainer is using the probability of
diabetes. Recall, precision, F1 and accuracy use a threshold of 0.5.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- An explainer wraps a fitted model with the data to explain it on and the true outcome; every explanation is then one function call.
- The outcome must be numeric, 1 for the event and 0 otherwise; check the explainer's report and the AUC before going on.
:::

### Part 2 — Global: which variables matter?

`model_parts()` computes the **permutation importance** of Exercise 9.1:
shuffle one variable, measure how much worse the model gets, repeat
(10 times by default) and average. DALEX measures "worse" with a **loss**,
which by default for a classifier is $1 - \text{AUC}$, so a larger loss is a
worse model. Two reference rows come with the result: `_full_model_`, the loss
with nothing shuffled, and `_baseline_`, the loss when *every* variable is
shuffled at once (a model that knows nothing, AUC about 0.5).

```{python}
importance_dalex = explainer.model_parts(random_state=1)

importance_dalex.result[["variable", "dropout_loss"]].round(3)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
result = importance_dalex.result
full_loss = result.loc[result["variable"] == "_full_model_", "dropout_loss"].iloc[0]
bars = result[~result["variable"].isin(["_full_model_", "_baseline_"])]
bars = bars.sort_values("dropout_loss")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.barh(bars["variable"], bars["dropout_loss"] - full_loss, left=full_loss, color="coral")
ax.axvline(full_loss, color="black", linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlim(left=full_loss - 0.01)                # leave room to see the dashed line
ax.set_xlabel("1 - AUC after shuffling the variable (dashed: no variable shuffled)")
ax.set_title("Random forest: permutation importance (DALEX)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# dalex's own plot gives the same picture, as an interactive plotly figure:
# importance_dalex.plot()
```

The full model has a loss of 0.176 (an AUC of 0.824). Shuffling glucose
raises it to 0.340; shuffling any other variable raises it by between
0.009 (pedigree) and 0.035 (BMI). This is the ranking of Exercise 9.1, Part 3, reached with
one line of code.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- `model_parts()` is permutation importance; its loss for a classifier is 1 − AUC, so higher means the model got worse.
- `_full_model_` and `_baseline_` frame the result: the loss with nothing shuffled, and with everything shuffled.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — How does the prediction change with one variable?

An importance says *how much* a variable matters, not *how*. A
**partial dependence profile** shows how: set glucose to 60 for every test
patient, keeping everything else about them as it is, and average the
predicted probabilities; then set it to 61, and so on, up to 199. The curve of
these averages is what the model predicts, on average, at each glucose level.

One patient's curve on its own (every other variable held at her values) is
an **individual conditional expectation (ICE)** or **ceteris-paribus** profile
("all else being equal"). The partial dependence profile is the average of the
150 ICE profiles.

```{python}
pdp_glucose = explainer.model_profile(variables=["glucose"], type="partial",
                                      verbose=False)

pdp_glucose.result.iloc[::20].round(3)   # every 20th of the 101 grid points
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(pdp_glucose.result["_x_"], pdp_glucose.result["_yhat_"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("Average predicted probability of diabetes")
ax.set_title("Partial dependence profile: glucose")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Up to a glucose of about 90 the curve stays between about 0.16 and 0.20. It
then climbs, gradually up to about 140 and steeply between 140 and 160, to
about 0.6, and stays between 0.6 and 0.66 above that. A logistic regression would have drawn a smooth S; the forest draws
steps, because it is made of splits.

Now the ICE profiles behind the average. They are stored in `raw_profiles`:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
ice = pdp_glucose.raw_profiles.result

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for patient_id in ice["_ids_"].unique():
    one = ice[ice["_ids_"] == patient_id]
    ax.plot(one["glucose"], one["_yhat_"], color="grey", alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(pdp_glucose.result["_x_"], pdp_glucose.result["_yhat_"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted probability of diabetes")
ax.set_title("ICE profiles (grey) and their average (blue)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Question!** Do all the grey curves have the same shape as the blue one? What
would it mean if some went up steeply and others hardly moved?

They rise in roughly the same place but by very different amounts, and they
start at different heights. Where ICE curves have different shapes, the effect
of glucose depends on the patient's other values: an **interaction**. The
average curve hides that, which is why it is worth drawing both.

**Your turn.** Draw the partial dependence profiles for the pedigree function
and for age. `model_profile()` takes several variables at once.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pdp_more = explainer.model_profile(variables=[______, ______], type="partial",
                                   verbose=False)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["pedigree", "age"]):
    one = pdp_more.result[pdp_more.result["_vname_"] == name]
    ax.plot(one["_x_"], one["_yhat_"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2)
    ax.set_xlabel(name)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Average predicted probability of diabetes")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
pdp_more = explainer.model_profile(variables=["pedigree", "age"], type="partial",
                                   verbose=False)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["pedigree", "age"]):
    one = pdp_more.result[pdp_more.result["_vname_"] == name]
    ax.plot(one["_x_"], one["_yhat_"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2)
    ax.set_xlabel(name)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Average predicted probability of diabetes")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In both languages the average prediction rises with the pedigree function,
from about 0.3 to about 0.5, most of the rise between 0.5 and 1.3. With age
it rises from about 0.25 at 21 to about 0.45 between 40 and 55, then falls
back to about 0.35. Only 6 of the 150 test patients are over 60 (and only 3
have a pedigree function above 1.2), so the right-hand ends of both curves
rest on very few people.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A partial dependence profile is the average prediction as one variable is moved through its range, everything else about each patient held fixed.
- ICE (ceteris-paribus) profiles are the individual curves behind that average; when their shapes differ, the variable interacts with others.
- A forest's profiles are step-shaped, because the forest is made of splits.
:::

### Part 4 — One patient: break-down and SHAP

`predict_parts()` explains one prediction. Take the first test patient again,
the 28-year-old with a glucose of 194 from Exercise 9.2.

```{python}
new_observation = test[predictors].iloc[[0]]

print(new_observation)
print(explainer.predict(new_observation))     # her predicted probability
```

**SHAP**, as in Exercise 9.2. DALEX estimates the Shapley values by adding the
variables in 25 random orders and averaging each variable's contribution, with
the 150 test patients as the background:

```{python}
shap_patient = explainer.predict_parts(new_observation, type="shap", B=25,
                                       random_state=1)

shap_average = shap_patient.result[shap_patient.result["B"] == 0]   # B = 0 holds the average over the 25 orders
shap_average = shap_average[["variable", "contribution"]]
shap_average.sort_values("contribution", key=abs, ascending=False).round(3)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3
ordered = shap_average.sort_values("contribution", key=abs)
colours = np.where(ordered["contribution"] > 0, "firebrick", "steelblue")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.barh(ordered["variable"], ordered["contribution"], color=colours)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("SHAP contribution to the predicted probability")
ax.set_title("SHAP values for the first test patient (dalex)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Glucose contributes +0.349, much as in Exercise 9.2 (+0.350
there). The numbers are not identical: the background is the test patients
rather than the training rows, and 25 random orders give an estimate, not the
exact value.

**Break-down** is the simplest way to share out a prediction: start from the
average prediction (the *intercept*), add the variables **one at a time** in a
fixed order, and record how much the average prediction moves at each step.
SHAP is the average of break-downs over many orders.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
breakdown_patient = explainer.predict_parts(new_observation, type=______)

breakdown_patient.result[["variable", "contribution", "cumulative"]].round(3)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
breakdown_patient = explainer.predict_parts(new_observation, type="break_down")

breakdown_patient.result[["variable", "contribution", "cumulative"]].round(3)
```

R: the intercept (the mean prediction over the 150 test patients) is 0.340;
glucose adds 0.324, then pedigree −0.013, pregnancies +0.019, age +0.076 and
BMI −0.055, ending at the prediction, 0.690. Python: intercept 0.338, glucose
+0.322, age +0.098, pregnancies −0.001, BMI +0.005, pedigree −0.073, ending
at 0.688. DALEX chooses the order itself, most influential first, so glucose
comes first in both and gets about the same contribution as its SHAP value.
The two forests order the remaining variables differently, and their
contributions change with the order.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The type is written as a string, with an underscore: look at the SHAP cell
above and at `help(explainer.predict_parts)`.
:::

**Question!** In the break-down, which variable comes first, and why does the
order matter? Would age get the same contribution if it were added first?

The contribution of a variable depends on what is already known when it is
added: knowing that a patient is 28 means something different before and
after you know her glucose is 194. Break-down picks one order; SHAP averages
over many, which is why it is the safer summary when variables interact.

All of these explanations, and more, can be browsed together in an
interactive dashboard:

```{python}
# Optional, not run here: an interactive dashboard of everything above
# arena = dx.Arena()
# arena.push_model(explainer)
# arena.push_observations(test[predictors])
# arena.run_server()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- `predict_parts()` explains one prediction; `type = "break_down"` adds the variables in one order, `type = "shap"` averages over many orders.
- When variables interact, a break-down depends on the order; SHAP removes that dependence by averaging.
- One explainer, four questions: how good is the model, which variables matter, how does the prediction change with a variable, and why did this patient get this prediction.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** The point of the exercise is the single interface: build
the explainer once, then ask four questions of it. Let students write the
`model_profile()` call for pedigree and age themselves before showing ICE.
The plots are drawn with ggplot2 / matplotlib from the result tables:
DALEX's own `plot()` methods (R) print ggplot2 deprecation warnings from the
ingredients package, and Python dalex draws interactive plotly figures that
do not render in a static page. Both are mentioned as comments.

**Changes from the original page.** The forest is fitted on the shared five
predictors and split (not all eight columns of `PimaIndiansDiabetes` with an
`initial_split`), without a normalising recipe (a forest does not need it, and
the profiles read in original units). The original passed
`y = as.numeric(test_data$diabetes)` for a factor with levels 0/1, which
gives 1 and 2; the explainer reported residuals with a mean of 1.01. Here `y`
is `as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos")`. The `vip` section of the original
page is in Exercise 9.1; `modelStudio` is a comment.

**Expected values.** R forest: accuracy 0.767, kappa 0.459, AUC 0.826; recall
0.547, precision 0.725, F1 0.624. Python: accuracy 0.760, kappa 0.451, AUC
0.824; recall 0.566, precision 0.698, F1 0.625. `model_parts()` mean dropout
loss (1 − AUC, 10 shuffles), R: full 0.174, pedigree 0.176, pregnant 0.188,
age 0.193, mass 0.210, glucose 0.334, baseline 0.505; Python: full 0.176,
pedigree 0.185, pregnant 0.193, age 0.208, mass 0.211, glucose 0.340,
baseline 0.506. Glucose partial dependence (grid 57 to 196), R: 0.210 at 57,
0.163 at 84.8, 0.296 at 113, 0.367 at 140, 0.612 at 168, 0.664 at 196;
Python: 0.196, 0.161, 0.304, 0.375, 0.592, 0.661. First test patient:
predicted 0.690 (R) / 0.688 (Python). DALEX SHAP (B = 25), R: glucose
+0.354, age +0.034, mass −0.026, pedigree −0.021, pregnant +0.010; Python:
glucose +0.349, age +0.048, pedigree −0.033, mass −0.020, pregnant +0.006.
Break-down, R: intercept 0.340, glucose +0.324, pedigree −0.013, pregnant
+0.019, age +0.076, mass −0.055, prediction 0.690. Python: intercept 0.338,
glucose +0.322, age +0.098, pregnant −0.001, mass +0.005, pedigree −0.073,
prediction 0.688. Only 6 of the 150 test patients are over 60.

**Common failures.** (1) `y = as.numeric(test$diabetes)`, giving 1/2. (2)
Passing the full test table, outcome included, as `data`. (3) In R, leaving
`N` at its default of 100: `model_profile()` then samples 100 of the 150
patients at random and the curve moves from run to run. (4) Reading the
right-hand end of the age profile as a real effect.

**Timing.** Part 1 fifteen minutes, Part 2 ten, Part 3 twenty, Part 4
twenty.
